1: Build instructions
2: ==================
3: 
4: Compiling TortoiseGit is not very difficult, but it requires several steps
5: to finish, at least the first time.
6: 
7: Unlike other big open source projects, once you have built all the libraries
8: TortoiseGit depends on, you can use the familiar Visual Studio IDE to build
9: and debug the binaries. No need to run the build script for every little change.
10: 
11: So don't give up if you read through the next section and all the requirements.
12: You only have to do this once.
13: 
14: Requirements
15: ------------
16: 
17: First, you need to install the compiler package:
18: 
19: *  You need at least Visual Studio 2022 for
20:    building the full TortoiseGit package.
21:    The TortoiseGit teams uses VS2022 Community Edition which is free for open-source
22:    projects (https://www.visualstudio.com/downloads/).
23:    Make sure you select the workload "Desktop development with C++" and the following components:
24:    * VC++ 2022 v143 toolset (x86,x64) (checked by default)
25:    * Visual C++ ATL-support (x86 and x64)
26:    * Visual C++ MFC support (x86 and x64)
27:    * Windows 11 SDK
28:    * optional: NuGet packet manager (requirement for GoogleTestAdapter, see below)
29:    * optional: GoogleTestAdapter (if you want to run the tests from within VS)
30:    * optional: CodeSigning certificate (for Windows 11 start menu extension)
31:    * For building ARM64 binaries (optional, also requires WiX >= 3.14):
32:      * VC++ 2022 v143 toolset ARM64 (newest)
33:      * Visual C++ ATL-support ARM64 (newest)
34:      * Visual C++ MFC support ARM64 (newest)
35: 
36: Next you might need to install some utilities/programs:
37: *  If you want to build the MSI installer you need WiX 3.11 (http://wixtoolset.org/releases/)
38:    and the VS2022 extension (https://github.com/wixtoolset/VisualStudioExtension/releases).
39: *  If you want to build the installer you need to update the PuTTY binaries by running ext/putty/download.bat
40: *  For building the docs you need NAnt (http://nant.sourceforge.net/), xsltproc,
41:    DocBook XSL for DocBook 5.x (https://cdn.docbook.org/release/xsl/),
42:    for spell checking you need aspell and for building PDF docs you need Apache fop (https://xmlgraphics.apache.org/fop/);
43:    all these prerequisite tools can be obtained packaged from https://sourceforge.net/projects/tortoisesvn/files/build%20tools/.
44:    Furthermore, Python 3 (can be installed from the Microsoft Store) is required.
45:    See doc/readme.txt for more details on building the docs.
46: 
47: In order to not build the Windows 11 start menu extension you need to adjust the following settings:
48: * Set BuildWindows11ContextmenuExtension to 0 in src/TortoiseGit.settings.props
49: * Unload the CustomActions11 project in the project explorer
50: 
51: In order to build the Windows 11 start menu extension you need to put your code signing certificate info into:
52: * src/TortoiseGitSetup/SparsePackage/AppxManifest.xml
53: * src/identity.manifest
54: 
55: Get external source code
56: ------------------------
57: 
58: TortoiseGit comes with all required code in its repository included or linked as submodules:
59: 
60: Run
61: 
62:     git submodule update --init
63: 
64: to download all linked repositories (submodules) automatically.
65: Alternatively, you can download submodules when cloning the main project with single command.
66: 
67:     git clone --recursive https://gitlab.com/tortoisegit/tortoisegit.git
68: 
69: 
70: After that you might need to apply TortoiseGit specific patches to the external libgit2 repository.
71: The patches, if any, are located in /ext/ and need to be applied to /ext/libgit2, e.g. using
72: 
73:     cd ext/libgit2
74:     for %%G in (..\libgit2-*.patch) do ( type %%G | git am --3way )
75: 
76: Building the packages
77: ---------------------
78: 
79: Open TortoiseGit.sln in Visual Studio.
80: Build all projects.
81: 
82: You can also build TortoiseGit via command line by calling MSBuild
83: Open Developer Command Prompt for VS20XX
84: 
85:     MSBuild TortoiseGit.sln /p:Configuration=Release;Platform=Win32
86:     MSBuild TortoiseGit.sln /p:Configuration=Release;Platform=x64
87: 
88: If you want to build the installer package, make sure you build the Win32 configuration before the x64 one
89: Also, build the docs before the installer packages (or copy existing TortoiseGit_en.chm and TortoiseMerge_en.chm files into the doc/output folder).

(End of file - total 89 lines)

1: Overall architecture of TortoiseGit
2: ===================================
3: 
4: Mainly TortoiseGit consists of several executables and two DLLs which
5: are of interest here (the project names are in parentheses bebind):
6: 
7: * TortoiseGit(32).dll (TortoiseShell)
8: * TortoiseGitStub(32).dll (TortoiseGitStub)
9: * TortoiseGitProc.exe (TortoiseGitProc)
10: * TGitCache.exe (TGitCache)
11: * TortoiseGitBlame.exe (TortoiseGitBlame)
12: * TortoiseGitIDiff.exe (TortoiseGitIDiff)
13: * TortoiseGitUDiff.exe (TortoiseGitIDiff)
14: * TortoiseGitMerge.exe (TortoiseGitMerge)
15: * TortoiseGitPlink.exe (TortoiseGitPlink)
16: * SshAskPass.exe (SshAskPass)
17: * GitWCRev.exe (GitWCRev)
18: * GitWCRevCOM.exe (GitWCRevCOM)
19: * tgittouch.exe (tgittouch)
20: 
21: TortoiseGit(32).dll and TortoiseGitStub(32).dll
22: ===============================================
23: These two files are the heart of the Explorer Shell extension.
24: TortoiseGitStub(32).dll is registered as a shell extension and
25: loads TortoiseGit(32).dll which finally provides the context menu
26: and overlay icons (in combination with TGitCache.exe).
27: 
28: TortoiseGit(32).dll checks which context menu items to show and when a
29: context menu item is clicked on, it calls TortoiseGitProc.exe which
30: handles all commands from the shell extension.
31: 
32: Why two dlls? The reason for TortoiseGitStub(32).dll is the setting
33: "Show overlays and context menu only in explorer". It checks whether
34: the parent process is explorer.exe and depending on the setting
35: TortoiseGit(32).dll gets loaded. - Before supporting this setting
36: TortoiseGit directly registered TortoiseGit(32).dll as the TortoiseGit
37: explorer shell extension w/o using TortoiseGitStub(32).dll.
38: 
39: TortoiseGitProc.exe
40: ===================
41: This is the main TortoiseGit GUI program. It is automatically executed
42: by the shell extension (TortoiseGit(32).dll) using command line
43: parameters indicating which action/command to execute and which files/folders
44: are selected in explorer.
45: 
46: If you want to see the command line parameters passed to TortoiseGitProc.exe
47: go to TortoiseGit settings, Advanced and set Debug to true. Starting from now
48: you will see all parameters passed to TortoiseGitProc.exe.
49: 
50: Some of the command line parameters (which we think are also useful for
51: users) are documented on
52: https://tortoisegit.org/docs/tortoisegit/tgit-automation.html#tgit-automation-basics.
53: 
54: If this program is started without any parameter, it just displays the about dialog.
55: 
56: Inside TortoiseGitProc all different commands have their own handler classes
57: and maybe dialogs (in MSVC you can see all the project directories for them).
58: Mostly TortoiseGitProc.exe will display its own dialogs and call git.exe. But for
59: diffing or blaming it will execute the other .exe files (such as TortoiseGitBlame.exe)
60: with appropriate command line parameters. Often TortoiseGitProc.exe also creates
61: temp files which are passed to the tools.
62: 
63: Noteworthy files
64: ----------------
65: Main class for functionality is AppUtils.cpp, which is called by many commands.
66: 
67: The log dialog and other revision lists are handled by GitLogListBase.cpp or
68: derived classes (context menu action handlers are in GitLogListAction.cpp).
69: 
70: GitStatusListCtrl.cpp is used everywhere where file lists are displayed
71: in dialogs, such as log dialog and commit dialog.
72: 
73: TGitCache.exe
74: =============
75: This is a process running in the background. It calculates working tree and
76: file statuses. The shell extension (TortoiseGit(32).dll) connects to it for
77: asking which overlay icons to show.
78: 
79: TGitCache also watches changes on folders which were opened in explorer before
80: in order to instantly react on changes and propagating updates of the overlay
81: icons to the shell extension.
82: 
83: For more information you can set the CacheTrayIcon setting to true in the
84: TortoiseGit advanced settings. After restarting TGitCache you can see a new
85: icon in the systray. Double clicking on it opens a window showing which files
86: TGitCache processes right now.
87: 
88: TortoiseGitBlame.exe
89: ====================
90: This program displays the blame functionality. It is called by TortoiseGitProc.exe
91: or manually by the user (there is an icon in the startmenu).
92: 
93: TortoiseGitIDiff.exe
94: ====================
95: This program is for comparing images. It is called by TortoiseGitProc.exe
96: or manually by the user (there is an icon in the startmenu).
97: 
98: Command line parameters are document here:
99: https://tortoisegit.org/docs/tortoisegit/tgit-automation-idiff.html
100: 
101: TortoiseGitUDiff.exe
102: ====================
103: This program is for showing .patch and .diff files with syntax highlighting.
104: It is called by TortoiseGitProc.exe or when the user double clicks on a .patch
105: or .diff file (TortoiseGitUDiff.exe is registered as a handler for these file
106: types on installation by default).
107: 
108: TortoiseGitMerge.exe
109: ====================
110: This program is for comparing files and resolving conflicts. It is called by
111: TortoiseGitProc.exe or manually by the user (there is an icon in the startmenu).
112: 
113: Command line parameters are document here:
114: https://tortoisegit.org/docs/tortoisegitmerge/tme-automation.html
115: 
116: SshAskPass.exe
117: ==============
118: This program is for providing a GUI for asking for credentials especially in
119: git.exe and ssh.exe.
120: 
121: Both, git.exe and ssh.exe (from OpenSSH) are command line tools. When executed
122: from TortoiseGitProc.exe there is no terminal attached and, thus, those tools
123: cannot ask for credentials. However, git.exe and ssh.exe allow to "register"
124: a helper utility (using the environment variables SSH_ASKPASS and GIT_ASKPASS).
125: 
126: All SshAskPass.exe does is, it displays the command line parameters in the GUI
127: and passes the entered values to STDOUT (where it is read by the calling tool).
128: 
129: GitWCRev.exe
130: ==============
131: This program is for reading the status of a Git working tree or specific files
132: inside a working tree, and performing keyword substitution in a template file.
133: 
134: This is a console command line program.
135: 
136: cf. https://tortoisegit.org/docs/tortoisegit/tgit-gitwcrev.html
137: 
138: GitWCRevCOM.exe
139: ==============
140: This program is the COM interface of GitWCRev.
141: 
142: cf. https://tortoisegit.org/docs/tortoisegit/tgit-gitwcrev-com-interface.html
143: 
144: tgittouch.exe
145: =============
146: This is a helper utility which creates/touches a file which is passed as
147: command line parameter.
148: 
149: It is needed for interacting with the Putty authentication agent (peagent).
150: TortoiseGit needs to know when the user finished entering his/her password,
151: but peagent is not blocking. Therefore, peagent is called with the private
152: key and tgittouch.exe together with a tmp filename.Then TortoiseGitProc.exe
153: waits untils the tmp-file is created.
